background.definition: Tinnitus is the perception of sound in one or both ears or in the head when no external sound is present. Symptoms can be unilateral or bilateral, present with or without hearing loss, and resemble ringing, hissing, whistling, humming, buzzing, chirping, or clicking sounds. Subjective tinnitus is the false perception of sound in the absence of an acoustic stimulus. Most tinnitus is considered subjective. Objective tinnitus is uncommon and results from noise generated by structures near the ear. Sometimes it is loud enough to be heard by the examiner.

list.listitem: The estimated prevalence of tinnitus ranges from 45 to 96 per 1000 persons according to data from the National Health Interview Survey.
40 million people are affected by tinnitus in the US.
In Canada 41% of those aged 3 to 79 years will experience tinnitus at least once in their lifetimes.

Subjective tinnitus: hearing loss, ototoxics, Meniere's disease, acoustic neuroma, multiple sclerosis, head injury, depression, anxiety, thyroid disorder, hyperlipidemia, vitamin B12 or zinc deficiency.
Objective tinnitus: arterial bruit, venous hum, arteriovenous malformation, vascular tumors, palatomyoclonus, idiopathic stapedial muscle spasm, patulous eustachian tube.

Selected ototoxics: aspirin, NSAIDs, aminoglycosides, chloramphenicol, erythromycin, tetracycline, vancomycin, various chemotherapy drugs, furosemide, bumetanide, chloroquine, mercury, lead, quinine, heterocyclic antidepressants.
Age-related hearing loss (presbyacusis) and noise exposure remain the most common causes.
Risk factors for tinnitus include age above 60, BMI of 30 kg/m2 or greater, smoking (former and current), diabetes mellitus, and hypertension.

Although pulsatile tinnitus is most often associated with vascular causes, idiopathic nonpulsatile tinnitus is thought to be due to a constellation of neural changes, including abnormal central processing and neural plasticity.
Avoid exposure to loud sounds, use ear plugs, and avoid ototoxic agents; if ototoxic drugs cannot be avoided, monitor drug levels. C
The USPSTF concludes that the current evidence is insufficient to assess the balance of benefits and harms of screening for hearing loss in asymptomatic adults aged 50 years or older.
The above recommendation is currently being updated by the USPSTF. Updates, when available, can be found by following reference.

Earplugs are effective in preventing temporary hearing loss in following loud music exposure.
Wear hearing protection, as needed.
Avoid ototoxic drugs, and check levels if they cannot be avoided.
Most cases of tinnitus are caused by SNHL. Dietary changes to reduce carbohydrate and cholesterol intake might prevent or delay the onset of SNHL.

list.listitem: A complete history and physical examination should be directed at determining the underlying cause of tinnitus. The history should include quality, duration, and frequency of tinnitus. Also evaluate the patient for hearing loss, vertigo, history of ear infections, trauma, and noise exposure.
A detailed medication history is important (see ).
A complete head and neck examination should be performed, including tuning-fork tests, a cranial nerve examination, and nasal endoscopy.
Auscultation over the neck, mastoid, and ear canal may reveal a carotid bruit or venous hum.
Weber and Rinne tests aid in the classification of sensorineural or conductive hearing loss ().
An obstructing mass, erythema of the canal or tympanic membrane, cholesteatoma, perforation, or effusion may be seen.
A glomus tumor presents as a red mass behind an intact tympanic membrane that blanches with positive pressure (Brown sign).
A red hue that overlies the promontory and does not blanch by pneumatoscope pressure is characteristic of the active phase of otosclerosis (Schwartze sign).
The cranial nerve examination (cranial nerves V, VIII, IX, X, or XI) may be asymmetric in the presence of vestibular schwannoma.
All patients should undergo audiometry with pure-tone threshold, speech discrimination, and tympanometry.
Laboratory evaluation to determine possible underlying etiologies may be considered (CBC, thyroid tests, lipid profile), but it is usually not helpful.

In patients with unilateral tinnitus and hering loss, rule out acoustic neuroma with gadolinium-enhanced MRI. In those with unilateral tinnitus and normal hearing and physical examination, MRI is not necessary unless tinnitus persists for more than 6 months.
Patients with visible evidence of a vascular tumor in the middle ear require CT, gadolinium-enhanced MRI, and referral to a subspecialist if the diagnosis is confirmed.

Those with pulsatile, objective tinnitus and no ear abnormalities on examination or audiology require further investigation of the vascular system with MRA. However, because MRA is not very sensitive for dural arteriovenous malformations, many clinicians then consider obtaining an arteriogram.
See algorithm in for suggested management.
See for a list of common ototoxic drugs.
Other than cognitive behavioral therapy, which has been shown to improve quality of life in those with tinnitus. Medicadtions lack evidence of benefit.B
Guidelines from UK NICE recommend imaging for patients with synchronous pulsatile tinnitus (tinnitus occurring with each heart beat), but only selectively for patients with nonpulsatile tinnitus.B
Guidelines from UK NICE recommend support for patients and their families, treatment for concomitant hearing loss, and psychological therapy for patients whose tinnitus is affecting their life.B
Although an association exists between tinnitus and depression, the direction of causality (if any) is unclear, and antidepressants have not been shown to improve tinnitus.
Patients with pre-existing anxiety and depression might beneft from SSRIs and TCA (tricyclic antidepressants).
Hyperbaric oxygen has been studied for the treatment of hearing loss and tinnitus but is not currently recommended.
Intratympanic dexamethasone injection for refractory tinnitus was found to be no better than intratympanic saline injection in a small double-blinded randomized trial.

A "neuroplasticity" drug D-cycloserine used in conjunction with cognitive training was no better than placebo at improving tinnitus bother, but was associated with improved self-reported cognitive problems in a RCT of 34 patients with tinnitus.
Ginkgo biloba has been found ineffective in the treatment of tinnitus.
Melatonin improves sleep and might improve tinnitus symptoms.

Sound-creating devices in the management of tinnitus in adults have not been shown to be more effective in decreasing the loudness or severity of tinnitus compared to other interventions such as patient education, relaxation techniques and counseling.

Pilot study of 46 patients with acute tinnitus, demonstrated that active transcutaneous electrical nerve stimulation (TENS) versus sham TENS was associated with improved symptom relief and quality of life after 4 weeks of treatment. No adverse events related to treatment occurred in either group.
A poor quality, small RCT found some benefit for the combination of Rosa canina, Urtica dioica, and Tanacetum vulgare in the treatment of non-pulsatile tinnitus.

UK NICE guidelines recommend offering virtual (Internet-based) psychological therapy, including cognitive behavioral therapy, acceptance and commitment therapy, and mindfulness-based therapies, to patients whose tinnitus is affecting their emotional and social well-being and daily activities.

Cognitive behavioral therapy has been found to significantly improve quality of life in those who suffer from tinnitus. It does not, however, decrease subjective volume of tinnitus, nor its associated depression. Studies have shown that CBT for tinnitus can be delivered using telemedicine with equivalent results based on multiple RCTs.
Patients with anxiety and those with severe tinnitus were more likely to respond to CBT.
In addition, there is some evidence that alternatives such as biofeedback-based and internet-based behavioral therapies improve qualitative measures of tinnitus.
There is insufficient evidence on the effectiveness of acupuncture in treating tinnitus.
UK NICE guidelines recommend amplification devices for patients with tinnitus and hearing loss.

Current guidelines suggest a multimodal approach for symptom relief, including patient education (on natural history and hearing protection), sound therapy (masking) to promote relaxation, and cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT); hearing aids are recommended if hearing loss is present.
Evidence does not support the use of pharmacologic agents, dietary supplements (e.g., ginkgo biloba), acupuncture, or nerve stimulation techniques for the treatment of tinnitus.
Reducing caffeine and alcohol consumption are often encouraged, along with adequate sleep and stress management based primarily on expert opinion.
Depending on the cause, subjective tinnitus is often intractable. Patients who undergo cognitive behavioral therapy may improve their ability to cope with chronic tinnitus. B

feature.caption: Rinne and Weber Tests to Evaluate Auditory Function.

tr.td: A vibrating tuning fork (either 256 or 512 Hz) is placed in the middle of the forehead equidistant from the patient's ears. The patient is asked to report in which ear the sound is heard louder.

In a normal patient, the sound is heard equally loud in both ears. However, a patient with symmetrical hearing loss will have the same findings. Thus, for the Weber test, there is diagnostic utility only in asymmetric hearing loss. A patient with a unilateral conductive hearing loss would hear the tuning fork loudest in the affected ear. If an occlusion is present, the sound cannot escape and appears louder on the ear with the conductive hearing loss. A patient with a unilateral sensorineural hearing loss would hear the sound louder in the unaffected ear, because the affected ear is less effective at picking up sound.
By placing a vibrating tuning fork (256 or 512 Hz) initially on the mastoid process until sound is no longer heard; the fork is then immediately placed just outside the ear.

Normally, the sound is audible at the ear. Air conduction uses the apparatus of the ear, eardrum, and ossicles to amplify and direct the sound whereas bone conduction bypasses this and allows the sound to be transmitted directly to the inner ear. In a normal ear, air conduction is better than bone conduction. In conductive hearing loss, bone conduction is better than air. In sensorineural hearing loss, bone conduction and air conduction are both equally depreciated.
